Question: “What are the landmark judgements in the retail home and furniture sector?”
Answer:
“Ajara Design Lounge Pvt. Ltd. v Ramesh Chandra Kapoor [First Appeal No. 536/2023, NCDRC]
The Complainant had filed a complaint against a home furnishing and interior design company alleging deficiency of service due to the company purchasing furniture and other fixtures from China without the consent of the Complainant, misrepresentation  with regards to the procurement of the furniture from unknown local third party vendors, and unfair demands of payment by the Opposite Party in contravention to the agreed upon payment terms. The District Commission had allowed the Complaint and granted compensation to the Complainant on the grounds that the Opposite Party had failed to provide any invoice/bills of purchase of the furniture to the Complainant as well as having made the purchases without the consent of the Complainant.

On appeal filed by the Opposite Party, the Commission reiterated the purpose of the enactment of the Consumer Protection Act - i.e., to protect the interests of the consumers and noted that the CDRCs have been conferred similar powers under Section 13 (4) of the CPA as that of a Civil Court under the Civil Procedure Code. The court also noted that CDRCs possess the jurisdiction to decide issues of ‘unfair trade practice’, defined under Section 2(r) of the CPA, which has a similar definition to “fraud” - defined under Section 17 of the Contracts Act. The Commission thus reiterated the position that complicated questions of fact involving ‘fraud’ can be decided by Consumer Dispute Redressal Commissions. Therefore, the Commission reaffirmed the order of the District Commission granting compensation to the Complainant for deficiency of service and hardship endured.

Seema Chandra v. Magnum Interiors Pvt Ltd [CC No. 1209/2015. NCDRC]
The Complainant had filed a complaint against an interior decorating company alleging deficiency of service for delay in completing the furnishing and interior decoration of her apartment. While dismissing the complaint, the court noted that the Opposite Party’s defence that the Complainant had delayed payment for the raw material, furniture, etc as per the time schedule fixed under the contract between them held merit. The Commission noted that the Complainant had failed to adduce any evidence of such payment to the Opposite Party nor produce any evidence to prove the Opposite Party’s liability and since the burden of proof was on the Complainant to prove deficiency of service, failure to prove this burden resulted in dismissal of the complaint of deficiency of service.

Shiva Real Estate (Comfort Homes) vs Nitin Kumar [Revision Petition No. 995/2017, NCDRC]
The Complainant filed a complaint before the District Commission alleging deficiency of service on the part of the builder for poor quality of construction of the Complainant's newly purchased apartment. The Complainant alleged that the apartment had numerous defects including cracks in the walls, lack of lifts, lack of electricity connection, lack of modular kitchen, lack of clean water, lack of fire safety equipment, lack of texture painting of walls, construction of an additional 6th floor despite obtaining approval for only 5 floors, lack of street lights and power backup equipment, entry of sewage into the premises causing illness, lack of car parking, improper laying of floor tiles in the rear courtyard, peeling off of the paint from the walls due to seepage of water into the walls, lack of proper maintenance dispute payment of fee, and the fact that the covered area of the flat was lesser than promised by the Opposite Party.
The District Commission had allowed the Complaint after considering the evidence submitted by the Complainant such as the sale deed, photographs of defects, etc and granted compensation to the Complainant for deficiency of service and mental agony caused by the various defects in the purchased apartment. After the State Commission had dismissed the appeal filed by the Opposite Parties, a revision petition was filed before the National Commission. The National Commission dismissed the revision petition on the grounds that the order of the State Commission did not warrant any interference or suffer from any infirmity or erroneous exercise of jurisdiction or material irregularity.

A. Rajender vs. The Interior Park Furniture Mall [C.C.No. 249 /2019, DCDRC, Hyderabad.]
In the case of A. Rajender vs. The Interior Park Furniture Mall decided on 25 January 2021, the complainant alleged that the furniture mall delivered a sofa set that did not match the agreed specifications and was also incomplete in installation, with a piece missing. Despite raising the issue, the seller failed to rectify the problem or provide a replacement. The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission found this to be a clear case of deficiency in service and unfair trade practice, ruling in favor of Mr. Rajender. The Commission ordered the furniture mall to replace the defective sofa set with the correct model, and also awarded ₹10,000 as compensation for mental anguish and ₹5,000 towards legal costs.

Question: “What is Food Safety?”
Answer: “The food safety sector in India encompasses regulations and standards to ensure the availability of safe, nutritious, and uncontaminated food for consumers. The aim is to protect public health by preventing the sale of adulterated, unsafe, or misbranded food. Food safety is a scientific field that outlines how to prepare, handle, and store food in order to avoid getting sick or contracting diseases from it. This includes a number of routines that should be followed to avoid potentially severe health hazards. Every consumer has a right to information about the safety and quality of the food they eat. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) is an independent organization created by the Indian government's Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. It was founded in accordance with India's Food Safety and Standards Act of 2006, which deals with food safety and regulation. The FSSAI is in charge of regulating and monitoring food safety in order to safeguard and advance public health.”

Question: “What is food?”
Answer: “ ‘Food’ means any substance, whether processed, partially processed or unprocessed, which is intended for human consumption and includes some primary food, genetically modified or engineered food or food containing such ingredients, infant food, packaged drinking water, alcoholic drink, chewing gum, and any substance, including water used into the food during its manufacture, preparation or treatment but does not include any animal feed, live animals unless they are prepared or processed for placing on the market for human consumption, plants, prior to harvesting, drugs and medicinal products, cosmetics, narcotic or psychotropic substances.”

Question: “What is food adulteration?”
Answer: “Food adulteration is the process in which the quality of food is lowered either by the addition of inferior quality material or by extraction of valuable ingredients. It not only includes the intentional addition or substitution of the substances but biological and chemical contamination during the period of growth, storage, processing, transport and distribution of the food products, is also responsible for the lowering or degradation of the quality of food products.”

Question: “What are adulterants?”
Answer: “Adulterants are those substances which are used for making the food products unsafe for human consumption and affects the retail public. As per the FSSA, 2006, “adulterant” means any material which is or could be employed for making the food unsafe or substandard or mis-branded or containing extraneous matter.”

These state authorities are responsible for enforcing food safety regulations at the local level, managing inspections, and addressing consumer complaints related to food safety within their jurisdiction.”

Question: What are the landmark judgements in this sector?
Answer:
“
HDFC Bank Limited and Ors. v. Hemant Narayan Devande
NCDRC observed that the denial of the transaction on a phone call by the Complainant shows that the petitioner bank must have come to know that the transaction was disputed. The Petitioner should have stopped the payment. NCDRC held deficiency in service on the part of the bank.

Renaissance Hotel Holdings, Inc. v. B.Vihaya Sai & Anr.
Regarding territorial jurisdiction- The place of business and place of work has to be understood not by looking at the booking through e-mails but where the actual physical business of hospitality is being done.

Spicejet Limited v. Ranju Aery
The Supreme Court ruled that consumers opting for online purchase of products through websites can file a consumer complaint before any consumer court for deficiency in services. Held that e‑commerce consumers can sue sellers anywhere, not just where the seller is based.

Flipkart Internet Pvt. Limited and Ors. Vs. Arun Kumar and Ors.
The complaint arose when the complainant ordered a mobile handset but received an old Nokia handset instead. Despite raising the issue with the opposite parties, the complainant was not provided with a resolution and his account was blocked.

The opposite parties contended that they were merely an online platform facilitating transactions between buyers and third-party sellers and thus should not be held liable for the issues arising from the product sold by the third party. However, it was found that the product delivered was different from what was ordered, establishing a deficiency in service. The Commission affirmed that the online platform must ensure proper delivery of products sold through its service.

Amazon Seller Services Pvt. Ltd. Vs. Jaspreet Kaur and Ors.
The issue involved the delivery of an incorrect product ordered by the complainant for ₹380 from OP 1. Upon receiving the wrong product, the complainant requested a replacement, which the OP denied, citing that the item had not been returned within the stipulated exchange window. While the OP did offer a full refund, the complainant insisted on a replacement instead.

The Commission held that given that the product was purchased through Amazon’s marketplace and the service “Fulfilled by Amazon” (FBA) was used, the court held that Amazon had a more active role in the transaction than just being a facilitator. Under the FBA program, Amazon stores, packs, and ships the products, thus assuming significant responsibility in the sale process. Moreover, the commission concluded that Amazon acted as an agent or representative of the seller (OP 2), and therefore could not absolve itself from liability for the incorrect product delivery. Amazon bore a responsibility to ensure that the product delivered to the complainant was the correct one, especially considering its involvement in the fulfilment process.

Yatin Sureshbhai Soni v. Union of India (2020): The Gujarat High Court addressed critical concerns regarding transparency and grievance redressal in the e-commerce sector. The petitioner, an advocate, filed a Public Interest Litigation seeking mandatory disclosure of essential product details like the country of origin, seller and importer information, and effective consumer grievance mechanisms on e-commerce platforms. The Court emphasized strict compliance with the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020—particularly the requirement for platforms to acknowledge complaints within 48 hours and resolve them within 30 days. It held that e-commerce entities, even when acting as intermediaries, could not evade responsibility if they played an active role in the sale or promotion of goods.

M/S Emaar MGF Ltd. v. Aftab Singh (2018): In this Supreme Court case, it was held that arbitration clauses in e‑commerce agreements do not bar consumer forum jurisdiction—consumers retain the right to pursue grievances through consumer courts regardless of such clauses.

Jatin Bansal v. Amazon Reseller Services Pvt. Ltd. (March 2024, NCDRC)
The commission held that Amazon’s “no return” clause on a mismatched item (a brand mismatch) is unfair and a deficiency of service under the Consumer Protection Rules, 2020. It affirmed that once the wrong item is delivered, Amazon is legally obligated to accept returns—even if its standard return policy doesn't explicitly cover it.

”

Question: “What are different payment methods available to consumers using e-commerce platforms?”
Answer:
“
Credit and Debit Cards
Major networks like Visa, Mastercard, American Express, and RuPay are widely accepted.
Often used for direct transactions and linked with features like EMI (Equated Monthly Installment) options.
2. Net Banking
Direct bank-to-bank transfers using online banking credentials.
Supported by almost all Indian banks and integrated with e-commerce payment gateways.
3. UPI (Unified Payments Interface)
A highly popular method in India, supported by apps like Google Pay, PhonePe, and Paytm.
Enables instant transfers using a Virtual Payment Address (VPA).
4. Wallets
Digital wallets like Paytm, MobiKwik, Amazon Pay, and others allow consumers to preload money or link their bank accounts for seamless transactions.
5. Cash on Delivery (COD)
A traditional but still prevalent option, particularly in regions where trust in online payments is low.
Allows payment in cash or card at the time of delivery.
6. Buy Now, Pay Later (BNPL)
Deferred payment options offered by companies like Simpl, LazyPay, or integrated BNPL features in platforms like Flipkart and Amazon.
Lets consumers pay after a specific period, often interest-free.
7. EMI (Equated Monthly Installments)
Available via credit cards or cardless EMI services like ZestMoney.
Helps consumers make high-value purchases by spreading payments over time.
8. Bank Transfers
Traditional NEFT, RTGS, and IMPS options for direct transfers to e-commerce entities.
10. Gift Cards and Vouchers
Prepaid instruments offered by platforms like Amazon and Flipkart, usable as payment for products or services.
11. International Payment Methods
For cross-border transactions, platforms may support PayPal, Skrill, or international credit cards.
12. Contactless Payments
NFC-enabled methods like Apple Pay and Samsung Pay for quick mobile payments, though adoption is still growing in India.
13. Cash on Delivery
Cash on Delivery (COD) is a payment method in e-commerce where the consumer pays for goods or services only upon receiving them. This method is particularly popular in regions where trust in online transactions or access to digital payment methods is limited.
The consumer can inspect the product before paying, ensuring trust in the transaction.
The payment can be made generally in cash, UPI, etc.

Question: “How are goods purchased on e-commerce generally shipped and delivered?”
Answer:
“
1. Order Fulfillment
Processing: Once an order is placed, it is confirmed and processed in the seller's or e-commerce platform's system.
Inventory Check: The product's availability is verified at the nearest warehouse or fulfillment center.
2. Packaging
The product is carefully packed to ensure safety during transit, often with eco-friendly or branded packaging.
3. Shipping
Third-party Logistics (3PL): Many platforms rely on logistics companies (e.g., IndiaPost, Blue Dart, DHL) to ship products.
In-house Logistics: Larger platforms like Amazon and Flipkart may have their own delivery networks (e.g. e-Kart logistics)
Shipping Modes:
Standard Delivery: Takes several days based on location.
Express/One-day Delivery: Premium service for faster delivery.
Cross-border Shipping: For international orders, requiring customs clearance.
4. Tracking
Consumers can track their orders via online platforms or mobile apps, which update the shipment status in real time.
5. Last-mile Delivery
Delivery Agents: Local delivery personnel handle the final leg of the journey, delivering the package to the consumer's address.
Contactless Delivery: Introduced during the COVID-19 pandemic, this option allows packages to be left at a designated spot without direct interaction.
Pickup Points: Some platforms offer delivery to lockers or specific pickup locations.
6. Proof of Delivery
Delivery may require:
A signature or OTP (One-Time Password) confirmation.
Photo evidence of the package at the destination (contactless).
7. Returns and Exchanges
If the product does not meet the consumer’s expectations, reverse logistics are initiated to pick up and return or replace the item.
”

Question: “What are the Product Liability & Penal Consequences for e-commerce sector?”
Answer: “The New Act has introduced the concept of product liability and brings within its scope, the product manufacturer, product service provider and product seller, for any claim for compensation. The term 'product seller' is defined to include a person who is involved in placing the product for a commercial purpose and as such would include e-commerce platforms as well. The defense that e-commerce platforms merely act as 'platforms' or 'aggregators' will not be accepted.”

Question: “What are the Duties of e-commerce entities?”
Answer:
“
An ecommerce entity shall:
a) Be  a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956 (1 of 1956) or the Companies Act, 2013 (18 of 2013) or a foreign company covered under clause (42) of section 2 of the Companies Act, 2013 (18 of 2013) or an office, branch or agency outside India owned or controlled by a person resident in India as provided in sub-clause (iii) of clause (v) of section 2 of the Foreign Exchange Management Act,1999 (42 of 1999); and
b) Appoint a nodal person of contact or an alternate senior designated functionary who is resident in India, to ensure compliance with the provisions of the Act or the rules made thereunder.
c) Provide the following information in a clear and accessible manner on its platform, displayed prominently to its users, namely:--
legal name of the e-commerce entity;
principal geographic address of its headquarters and all branches;
name and details of its website; and
contact details like e-mail address, fax, landline and mobile numbers of customer care as well as of grievance officer.

Every e-commerce entity shall establish an adequate grievance redressal mechanism having regard to the number of grievances ordinarily received by such entity from India, and shall appoint a grievance officer for consumer grievance redressal, and shall display the name, contact details, and designation of such officer on its platform.

Every e-commerce entity shall ensure that the grievance officer referred to in sub-rule (4) acknowledges the receipt of any consumer complaint within forty-eight hours and redresses the complaint within onement from the date of receipt of the complaint.

Where an e-commerce entity offers imported goods or services for sale, it shall mention the name and details of any importer from whom it has purchased such goods or services, or who may be a seller units platform.

Every e-commerce entity shall endeavor on a best effort basis to become a partner in the convergence process of the National Consumer Helpline of the Central Government.

3. No e-commerce entity shall—
adopt any unfair trade practice, whether in the course of business on its platform or otherwise.
Impose cancellation charges on consumers cancelling after confirming purchase unless similar charges are also borne by the e- commerce entity, if they cancel the purchase order unilaterally for any reason.
Record the consent of a consumer for the purchase of any good or service offered on its platform where such consent is expressed through an explicit and affirmative action, and no such entity shall record such consent automatically, including in the form of pre-ticked checkboxes.
manipulate the price of the goods or services offered on its platform in such a manner as to gain unreasonable profit by imposing on consumers any unjustified price having regard to the prevailing market conditions, the essential nature of the good or service, any extraordinary circumstances under which the good or service is offered, and any other relevant consideration in determining whether the price charged is justified;
Discriminate between consumers of the same class or make any arbitrary classification of consumers affecting their rights under the Act.
”

(2) Every marketplace e-commerce entity shall require sellers through an undertaking to ensure that descriptions, images, and other content pertaining to goods or services on their platform is accurate and corresponds directly with the appearance, nature, quality, purpose and other general features of such good or service.

Question: “What are the Duties of sellers on the marketplace?”
“If I click ‘I agree’ to a website’s terms and conditions while shopping online, am I legally bound by those terms?”
Answer:
“ Yes, when you click “I agree” to a website’s terms and conditions during an online purchase, you are generally entering into what is known as a clickwrap agreement—a type of contract that is legally recognized in India. Under Indian law, especially the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a contract becomes valid when there is mutual consent, a lawful object, and an intention to create legal obligations. The Information Technology Act, 2000 further supports the validity of electronic contracts by recognizing digital communication and click-based consent as legally enforceable. So, by clicking “I agree,” you are usually seen as having accepted the terms, even if you didn’t read them word for word.
That said, not all terms in these agreements are automatically enforceable. The law makes a distinction between valid consent and unfair or one-sided contract terms. Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, especially Section 2(46), any term that significantly disadvantages the consumer—like a no-refund clause for defective goods, excessive cancellation charges, or making returns nearly impossible—can be considered an unfair contract term. Indian courts and consumer commissions have struck down such terms when they’ve been found to be exploitative, misleading, or hidden in fine print.
Also, if the design of the website makes it hard for you to understand what you’re agreeing to—like using small fonts, complicated language, or interface tricks to hide important terms—those practices may also be legally challenged. The Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns (2023) now make it illegal for platforms to mislead consumers using manipulative designs or unclear consent flows.
So, while clicking “I agree” generally means you’ve accepted the contract, it does not mean that businesses can get away with unfair conditions. If the terms are unreasonable, not clearly explained, or against your basic rights as a consumer, you have legal grounds to raise a complaint or seek redressal through a consumer forum.
Related Case: M/S Emaar MGF Ltd. v. Aftab Singh (2018)
In this Supreme Court case, it was held that arbitration clauses in e‑commerce agreements do not bar consumer forum jurisdiction—consumers retain the right to pursue grievances through consumer courts regardless of such clauses.
”
